title: Five Things CEOs Can Learn About AI from Asia-Pacific
gist: BCG argues that Asia-Pacific CEOs are compounding a durable AI advantage over wait-and-see Western peers by personally owning AI transformation, building proprietary 'business-context layers' around off-the-shelf models, and concentrating on one or two large initiatives rather than thousands of pilots. The implied investment view: enterprise AI value accrues to the owners of proprietary context and process data, not to whoever rents the frontier model, and cheap or open-weight models are often good enough.

insights.claim: BCG research finds Asia-Pacific CEOs are confident and optimistic about achieving positive ROI on AI, and BCG argues each quarter a Western CEO spends in wait-and-see mode lets leading Asia-Pacific companies compound their advantage.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: If AI advantage compounds with time-in-market rather than model access, relative AI capex/adoption timing becomes a regional equity differentiator — watch Asia-Pacific corporates versus Western laggards on realized AI ROI disclosures.
insights.quote: every quarter a CEO in the West spends in wait-and-see mode is another quarter that leading companies in Asia-Pacific compound their advantage
insights.locator: CEOs in Asia-Pacific are confident about AI

insights.claim: Asia-Pacific CEOs are described as personally briefed on both Silicon Valley and China — often having visited Silicon Valley within the prior month — and BCG recommends Western leadership teams and boards physically visit China to experience its digital consumer market.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Implies Western boards systematically underrate Chinese digital-consumer capability; a case that China tech/consumer platforms are under-benchmarked by Western allocators even amid decoupling rhetoric.
insights.quote: Leadership teams, CEOs, and boards of Western companies should visit China to live the digital consumer experience a little and broaden their lens.

insights.claim: BCG's framework holds that AI-driven product development does not converge across companies because LLMs are applied on top of a company-specific 'business-context layer' of proprietary consumer insights, processes, and flows — so identical models produce different outputs.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Supports the view that enterprise AI value accrues to owners of proprietary process/consumer data rather than to model vendors — favors data-rich incumbents and context/orchestration tooling over commoditized model access.
insights.quote: the large language models (LLMs) it uses are accessing a very specific business-context layer

insights.claim: Because the context layer takes time to build, leading companies are building it now instead of waiting for the next GPT or LLM iteration — BCG likens delaying AI transformation for better technology to skipping the gym this year because better equipment arrives next year.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Argues enterprise AI adoption is not deferrable by a model-upgrade cycle; a headwind to the 'wait for the next model' capex-pause thesis and supportive of sustained enterprise AI services demand.
insights.quote: Delaying an AI transformation while waiting for better technology is a bit like not going to the gym this year because there will be better exercise equipment next year.
insights.locator: But it takes time to build this layer

insights.claim: BCG observes that most companies driving AI transformation use multiple foundation models and that a good-enough model is often sufficient, with many keeping expensive models alongside open-source or open-weight models in their 'model gardens.'
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Directly challenges frontier-model pricing power: enterprise workloads routed to cheaper/open-weight models compress inference revenue per seat and favor inference infrastructure and routing layers over any single model vendor.
insights.quote: Sometimes a Toyota rather than a Ferrari is the car to drive to work every day.
insights.locator: Pick More Than Just One Model

insights.claim: BCG prescribes setting AI KPIs in the 50%-plus improvement range — such as performing R&D 50% faster or achieving 50% higher return on advertising spend — on the grounds that only targets that large force a reshaping of core functions.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete benchmark for screening corporate AI disclosures: claimed gains far below 50% in core functions suggest pilot-level activity rather than genuine transformation.
insights.quote: set KPIs that are in the 50%-plus range
insights.locator: Then, set KPIs that are in

insights.claim: BCG identifies the 'pilot trap' — thousands of pilots that do not add up — and says companies succeeding with AI in Asia-Pacific instead pick one or two massive initiatives and concentrate investment there.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for whether a company's AI spend will show up in margins: concentrated flagship programs, not pilot counts, are the signal of eventual P&L impact.
insights.quote: picking one or two massive initiatives and investing in those instead of having thousands of pilots that do not add up to anything

insights.claim: BCG says it has yet to encounter a company with fully clean and organized data, and that unstructured inputs such as meeting notes or factory-floor standup transcripts can be processed quickly to drive AI use cases — so waiting for data readiness is itself the error.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Removes 'our data isn't ready' as a credible deferral excuse and shortens the assumed lead time between enterprise AI spend and measurable value — bullish for near-term enterprise AI deployment volumes.
insights.quote: If you wait for all the data to be ready, you’ll never get started.
insights.locator: The second is the data trap

insights.claim: BCG argues CEOs should personally own AI initiatives rather than devolving responsibility to the CIO or technology function, selecting targets by asking which functions, if improved, would win market share or lower costs.
insights.speaker: Jeff Walters
insights.so_what: Governance tell for investors: AI programs owned by the CIO rather than the CEO are more likely to stay cost-center pilots than to reshape core economics.
insights.quote: avoid devolving responsibility to the CIO or technology function
insights.locator: Take the Lead to Truly Reshape Your Business
